There are a few things that matter when it comes to testing the best infrared heaters. For one, they must be safe, so they need a sturdy build and/or safety features. Next, they need to produce the right amount of heat.

To test them, we set up each of the heaters according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Some could sit on the floor, while others needed to hang from the wall or the ceiling. We set them up, turned them on, and checked features like remote controls and timers.

First, we examined each radiant heater to see how sturdy or secure it appeared to be. If a heater could tip over, we made sure the safety shutoff worked. We also cranked the heaters as high as they could go to check the surfaces around the mounted heaters for safe temperatures.

Next, we checked the output. We turned each electric infrared heater up to the max setting to see how quickly they’d heat up, and we played with the thermostats to ensure they were working properly. From there, we compared the design and build quality between each model.

Infrared rays are uniquely capable of cutting through empty space and bringing warmth to the objects they strike; in fact, that’s how the sun heats the earth. Today’s infrared heaters bring warmth to objects, like clothes and skin rather than the surrounding air—an efficient mechanism in stark contrast to convection heaters, which warm the surrounding air before heating objects in that space.

Although heating the air may distribute heat more uniformly throughout a room, much energy is wasted heating unoccupied space, such as high ceilings or the outdoor air. Infrared heaters use 100 percent of the heat they produce to bring focused warmth to the objects in the path of its rays, making them much more energy efficient. An infrared heater’s energy efficiency, space coverage, and other features will vary depending on certain factors. Shoppers may want to keep the following considerations in mind while on the hunt for the best infrared heater for their homes.

When determining the right size of an infrared heater to buy, think about the square footage of the space you want to warm. Generally, infrared heaters are relatively small and portable. More powerful units for bigger areas are available, but they’re typically larger. Also, consider how much floor space an infrared heater will take up; this will vary depending on whether the unit sits vertically (in the case of a tower heater) or horizontally (like most standard heaters).

The size of the space you want to warm will also influence how powerful your heater should be. The amount of heat generated by these devices, measured in BTUs, influences the size of the space they can heat.

The BTU output of an infrared heater generally correlates with the number of watts the heater uses, which can range between 300 and 1,500 watts. (Most are capped at 1,500 watts because that’s the maximum amount a standard 110V household electrical outlet can handle.) With convection space heaters, 1 watt is equivalent to 3.412 BTUs, so it’s simple to determine the size of a space they can warm; it’s not so easy with infrared heaters.

Infrared heaters can use various heating elements, such as quartz (the most common and most efficient), ceramic, and carbon, to produce and emit infrared rays with varying levels of energy efficiency. Supplemental fans or blowers aren’t necessary, but they can provide both focused infrared heat and diffused heat through convection.

These factors impact how an infrared heater’s power rating will affect its heat output and space coverage. Just because an infrared heater boasts a higher power rating doesn’t mean it produces more heat and provides greater space coverage—much depends on the individual characteristics of the heater.

One way to calculate the general amount of power a heater should generate is to multiply the space’s square footage by 10. For example, a 100-square-foot room (10 feet by 10 feet) will need a 1,000-watt heater (100 x 10 = 1,000).

The location of an infrared heater warrants consideration due to its unique heating action. Whether it’s for outdoor use or a space heater for a basement, generally, it’s a good idea to place an infrared heater directly in front of what you want to warm. But, to be on the safe side, we consulted HVAC expert Bohannon to see where infrared heaters should be placed, and he recommends that “infrared heaters should not be placed near flammable materials such as curtains, furniture, or paper,” he says. He adds to always maintain adequate clearance around the heater to avoid any fire hazards. “It’s also important to follow the manufacturer’s guidelines regarding safe distances from walls and other objects,” Bohannon says.

The fact that they operate by emitting heat waves directly to objects (as opposed to the surrounding air) also makes them well suited to outdoor spaces, such as patios, since the heat won’t dissipate in the surrounding air. Similarly, infrared heaters are a good option for rooms with large ceilings since users needn’t worry about heated air rising and wasting away in the ceiling space.

An infrared heater needn’t be an eyesore, as there are various designs to complement different styles of home decor. Shoppers can find heaters with wood, plastic, and metal finishes, all in various colors.

The shape of the heater will depend on whether it sits on the floor vertically or horizontally, which affects not only its function but its visual form as well. Some infrared heaters simulate the appearance of a fireplace with visual and auditory effects like flames and crackling.

Infrared heaters can range from highly portable to completely stationary units. The majority are for supplemental space heating, so they’re usually portable. Some models are portable by design; they’re tidily compact and include carry handles and caster wheels. Handles and wheels are helpful for larger, heavier units that would otherwise be difficult to move. Other models, like those that hang from the wall and ceiling, aren’t portable at all.

Space heaters are a leading cause of house fires, so choosing an infrared heater with safety features is important. This is especially true for homes with pets or children who could knock the unit over. Fortunately, many manufacturers do incorporate several safety features, including:

Look for a heater with at least two of these safety features, but the more, the better. For added confidence, find a heater that’s certified by a third-party inspection agency, such as Underwriter Laboratory (with a UL logo), Intertek (stamped with the letters ETL and corresponding logo/emblem), or Canadian Standards Association (stamped with a CSA logo/emblem).

Some infrared heaters boast bells and whistles to increase functionality. These may include:

Energy-efficient infrared heaters are capable of heating the objects in a space more quickly than other types of heaters, such as convection-style units that must warm the surrounding air before they can heat the objects. They’re also usually quieter than other heaters since they don’t require fans—and those units that do have fans aren’t usually very loud. The warmth infrared heaters create won’t increase humidity or dry the air in the room, so the heat is more comfortable. Other benefits include:

If you still have questions about infrared heaters, see the answers to some common questions below for greater clarity.

No. In fact, they can use considerably less than other heaters because of how efficiently they heat up a space.

While infrared heaters are intrinsically safer than most other types of heaters, they should only be left on overnight if they have integrated safety features like an automatic tip-over shutoff, an overheat shutoff, and a shut-off timer.

Infrared heaters should only be used in the locations they are designed for. Consequently, only infrared wall heaters should be mounted on a wall.

Infrared heaters provide direct heat, so you’ll want to place it facing the area where you want to concentrate the warmth. Make sure there aren’t obstructions in the way.

Expect home infrared heaters to last about the same amount of time as other space heaters; a few years, with some good products (that are also well taken care of) lasting over a decade.

Yes, it’s possible to heat an entire house with infrared heating. However, it is usually done with larger infrared heating panels, not the more compact units like those on this list. The smaller heaters in this guide are best for supplementary heating, as a toasty addition to your home heating system.

#7754. Journal of Free Speech Law: "Protecting the Thinking Process in Human-AI Interaction: The Forum Interstitiale Between Thought and Expression," by Caroline De Cock

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

International human rights law protects freedom of thought absolutely and freedom of expression subject to limitations. The relevant established doctrine calls the two sides of that line the forum internum and the forum externum. However, the line was drawn when thinking left no trace, and with current technological developments, it no longer holds.

Within the span of six months in 2026, a United States court ordered that 20 million ChatGPT conversations be provided as evidence under ordinary discovery rules, two federal courts reached opposite conclusions on whether a litigant's exchanges with a chatbot were protected at all, and the Supreme Court held that location records kept by a third party remain constitutionally protected. Records of where a person's body had been were protected, while records of how their mind worked were not.

The law currently has no category for the search query, the exploratory prompt, the unfinished draft, or the confession made to a machine. The U.S. answer has been a quarrel about privilege: Courts refuse to grant AI exchanges between users and chatbots protection because the machine is not a professional, like a doctor or a lawyer, and the industry asks for a new privilege because it claims the model behaves like one. Both the courts and the industry assume that protection depends on what the person is using, i.e., what the machine is. This Article argues that it depends on what the person who uses the machine is doing.

It proposes the forum interstitiale, a third zone between the two classical fora, which can protect the thinking process under a standard stronger than ordinary expression law but short of absolute. Every candidate analogy to interactions with AI chatbots in existing law is tested herein, from search queries and confidential dialogue to protected reading, aggregated records, the European law on correspondence and data protection, private diaries and drafts, and neural data. Each fails for the same reason, namely that the protection it offers relates to a relationship, a disclosure, a recording, an addressee, or a data type, and never to the function of the act as thinking.

The interstitial zone this Article proposes only flows upwards. It lifts acts abandoned by the current binary approach into protection and displaces nothing from the absolute core of protected thought. The Article also sets out what acts belong in the liminal zone, five elements of the protection standard, the duties those elements impose on AI providers, and a map of individual AI interactions across the three fora. This classification determines what records of thought can be demanded, kept, filtered, and used against the person who was engaged in the process of thinking.

#7753. What Is “Heart Attack Snow,” and Why Is It So Dangerous?

Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk. Learn why people call it heart attack snow and how to shovel safely.

Shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore. Icy walkways can cause serious falls, and prolonged exposure to the cold can lead to hypothermia or frostbite. Another safety concern is something called “heart attack snow.”

The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter. For those in snowy climates, understanding the risks of heart attack snow is important before picking up a shovel.

Understanding the risks can help prevent a routine chore from becoming a medical emergency.

Heart attack snow is a nickname for heavy, wet snow that’s harder to shovel than dry, powdery snow. The name comes from the strain that lifting this type of snow can place on the heart. According to the National Weather Service, snow with a higher water content weighs more, making each shovelful harder to lift.

The added effort can quickly raise heart rate and blood pressure. Cold temperatures also cause blood vessels to narrow, making the heart work harder. The American Heart Association warns that this combination can trigger a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest.

The association says the risks are especially concerning for “people who already have cardiovascular risks like a sedentary lifestyle or obesity,” including those with a history of smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, or high blood pressure. People who have previously suffered a heart attack or stroke also face greater risks.

Even lighter, powdery snow can be dangerous, especially when large amounts require repeated lifting or hours of clearing.

Before heading outside, people should warm up indoors and stretch gently. Dressing in layers helps protect against the cold, while staying hydrated is important even when someone doesn’t feel thirsty.

The American Heart Association recommends pushing snow rather than lifting it whenever possible. When lifting is necessary, smaller loads and frequent breaks can help limit physical strain. A snow blower can also reduce the amount of lifting, although operating one still requires effort.

Slippery surfaces are another concern. “Walking on ice is extremely dangerous,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency recommends using rock salt or another de-icing product to keep walkways clear of ice. Sand can also help prevent slipping.

People with heart disease or significant cardiovascular risk factors should have someone else handle snow removal, according to the American Heart Association.

Recognizing the warning signs of a heart attack is equally important. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, cold sweats, or discomfort in the arms, back, or jaw can all signal a serious problem. Symptoms aren’t always severe and can vary from person to person.

Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms should stop shoveling immediately and call 911. The American Heart Association advises against waiting to see whether symptoms go away.

Unfortunately, the following two LED light strips we tested didn’t make our list:

To test the best LED light strips, we installed them in appropriate places, including our kitchen, office, TV, and car. We also spoke with Dara Greaney, CEO and founder of LED Light Expert, who provided some sage advice for shoppers. “Strip lights are a fun DIY project, but they are not plug and play. You need to figure out how to secure them, where to power them, and how to cut them if necessary.”

Then, over the following 2½ weeks, we used the light strips via remote and app to test their features and functionality. We set lighting schedules, created lighting themes, and used the lights in real-life situations. We rated each set according to installation, illumination, and durability criteria. After rating the lights on a scale of 0 to 4, we calculated their scores and assigned the worthy options awards.

There are many features to consider when shopping for the best LED strip lights, from color and size to intended use and brightness. Before shoppers purchase an LED light strip, they will want to keep the following factors in mind to ensure their choice meets or exceeds their expectations for the intended application.

It’s essential to determine where the LED light strip will be installed before deciding which product to purchase. Some designs are for specific purposes, such as stair lighting or television backlighting. This specialization differentiates those products from standard LED light strips.

For example, a product intended for backlighting a TV may come with four precut pieces and television-specific syncing options that change color to mimic the colors on the screen. Other location considerations include water resistance for patios, dimmer compatibility for bedrooms, or motion sensing for a hall, bathroom, or stairway.

Light strips are available in a variety of lengths, typically from 1 to 32 feet, though some strips run up to 50 feet long or more. The brightness and intended purpose usually correlate to their length. For example, LED light strips intended for television backlighting or use on stairs tend to be shorter for easier installation.

Low-brightness LED light strips can be up to 32 feet long with about 300 LED lights. High-brightness LED light strips may have the same number of LED modules, but they’ll usually only be about 16 feet long. However, most flexible LED strip lights can be cut using scissors to accommodate small areas. If longer LED tape is needed, check to see if you can connect pieces to create the desired length.

Most light strips feature a flexible circuit board that can bend around corners or run over curved surfaces. Some LED light strips are so flexible that they can be bent up to 90 degrees without damaging the circuit board.

However, as the power of an LED light strip increases, the flexibility decreases, with some light strips being completely rigid in design. These inflexible products tend to be much shorter, sometimes only 1 foot long, and significantly brighter than the average light strip. They can also feature motion-sensing technology, making them ideal for lighting stairs.

As with LED light bulbs, the brightness of an LED light strip is measured in lumens and is dictated by the density of the LED lights within 1 meter.

Ideal brightness can be challenging to figure out, and some manufacturers don’t include this information. By taking note of the LED density, you can determine the average brightness of the light strip. Most light strips come in two densities: standard density (SD) of 30 LEDs per meter (9.1 LEDs/foot) or high density (HD) of 60 LEDs per meter (18.3 LEDs/foot).

SD light strips produce an average of 540 lumens and need 27 watts of power. They can be up to 32.8 feet long. HD light strips provide an average of 1,080 lumens, need 40 watts of power, and come in a maximum length of 16.4 feet.

Some light strips come in only one color, while others can have color selections that range in the millions. The color option chosen is entirely dependent on personal preference.

Color temperature in various types of light bulbs is measured in degrees Kelvin (K) and describes how warm or cool a light’s color appears; lower numbers indicate warmer color temperatures. The soft glow of an average incandescent light bulb is a warm temperature of 2,700K, while natural daylight is much cooler, averaging 6,500K.

We interviewed interior decorator Vivianne Chow, the owner of Viv and Tim Home in Chicago, on this subject. She shared some expert advice. “Make sure that the color temperature of the LED light strips matches what you currently have at home. I recommend sticking to 2700K or 3000K for a warm white look instead of 5000K, which is a little bit too cool-toned.”

Wattage measures how much energy the light strip requires to function at its optimal brightness. If a light strip requires more energy than the power source can provide, it won’t work correctly, causing the light produced to be weak. LED light strips generally operate using batteries or power adapters plugged into wall outlets, but some options can be hardwired directly into the home’s electrical system.

LED light strips with lower brightness requirements, such as a 540-lumen strip, will also have reduced wattage requirements. As brightness demands increase, power demands also rise, with a 16.4-foot SD light strip requiring 27 watts of power and a 16.4-foot HD LED light strip requiring 40 watts.

In our interview with Dara Greaney, he also mentioned that “LEDs are 90 percent more efficient than incandescent and 60 percent more than CFL/fluorescent, so anytime we use LEDs we are saving money and going green.” LED lights are certainly something to consider for energy-conscious consumers.

In years past, LED light strips were hardwired into the electrical system to work with a light switch or plugged into a power outlet and controlled with a button. However, LED light strips have come a long way from their original design.

Light strips are available that connect to Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or remotes. With these controls, you can adjust brightness and color, program the lights to sync with music, or set schedules for waking up, arriving home from work, or going to sleep.

LED light strips that connect with smart-home devices like Amazon Alexa or Google Home can even be controlled using voice commands, while more straightforward options with just one color may only have a remote to turn the light on or off.

LED light strips come with many pros and a few cons. Whether you’re looking for LED strip lights for bedrooms, LED strip lights for kitchen cabinets, or bedroom LED light strips, the answers to these common questions may help.

LED light strips are safe as long as they’re installed and operated according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For example, indoor lights shouldn’t be installed outside, and some lights should not be installed where they can get wet.

LED light strips can run for hours on end without being shut off. They get warm, but they’re designed to underdrive the LEDs, meaning they don’t put out much heat. This makes them nice ambient or task lighting but not ideal as LED grow lights.

Yes, you must plug in most LED light strips. We did test one battery-operated cordless model, but it was a short 16-inch strip. However, this non-electric option would be a reliable light during a power outage.

Almost every LED strip is compatible with a dimmer switch. To make an LED light strip dimmable, you must first connect its input wire to a dimmer unit and then connect the unit to the power supply.

To create ambient light in your home with LED strip lights, the optimal locations are under or above cabinets and counters in the kitchen, behind mirrors in the bathroom, or even around large pieces of furniture like bookshelves and home entertainment units.

LED strip lights can be disposed of by taking them to a local recycling center.

LED lights are built to last, with most LED light strips lasting for up to 50,000 hours of use, which is roughly 10 to 20 years of runtime.

#7749. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.

#7748. Will Alito or Thomas Retire if Democrats Win the Senate?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

While the Ginsburg example looms in the background, the answer depends on what values the justices are trying to maximize

Will Justice Thomas and/or Alito retire if Democrats take the Senate in tomorrow's election, hoping that the lame-duck Senate will confirm a nominee chosen by President Trump? In recent conversations, I've heard increasing speculation and support for this possibility among some judicial conservatives. And I hear corresponding worry among progressives.

Both sides think the election may create a brief, very consequential window for a Republican Senate to replace two aging justices. The GOP Senate would have to confirm their replacements before January 3, 2027. There would be political costs and procedural obstacles, but it could be done. Justice Barrett was confirmed by a Republican Senate within a month of her nomination on the eve of the 2020 election.

The rationale for retirement is straightforward: Don't get trapped in the actuarial straitjacket Justice Ginsburg found herself in when she failed to retire in 2014 (when she was 81). That was her last clear chance of retiring with a Democratic president and Senate.

Thomas is 78. Alito is 76. Neither has disclosed a serious health risk, and both have indicated they have no plans to retire this year.

But if Democrats take the Senate (prediction markets currently give them a 75% chance to do so) and if they play the sort of constitutional hardball over Supreme Court confirmations that Republicans have played in the past ten years, there's very little chance the new Senate would confirm any likely Trump nominee. Democrats needn't reject every possible Trump nominee--just those who would be likely to satisfy the conservative legal movement. So the president might not get another Supreme Court appointment before he leaves in January 2029. Calls for the eldest conservative justices to retire would surely intensify.

It's worse than that for judicial conservatives. If a Democrat wins the White House in 2028, the next opportunity for a Republican president to make an appointment might not come until January 2033. There are some important "ifs" packed in there, but they are well within the range of reasonable possibilities.

In January 2033, Thomas would be 84, Alito 82. Even assuming both remain healthy and active, that's a substantial amount of succession risk for conservatives to accept when they could potentially lock in their seats for another generation this winter.

A rational justice who prioritizes preserving his seat for something close to his judicial philosophy might well retire. But a rational justice might prioritize (or at least see himself as prioritizing) other things: continued service, jurisprudential influence, institutional reputation, and personal legacy. Justices do not see themselves simply as strategic agents of the political coalitions that produced their appointments.

For purposes of predicting what Alito and Thomas might do, the Ginsburg example cuts both ways. It illustrates the risks of refusing to retire when one's political allies control the presidency and Senate. At the same time, it illustrates the limits of assuming justices will subordinate their personal preferences regarding tenure, legacy, and judicial responsibility to the interests of that coalition.

Like Ginsburg, Thomas and Alito would probably resist renewed and intense calls for their immediate retirement. They might figure that:

(1) one of those additional "ifs" won't come to pass—that Republicans will retake the Senate in '28 or retain the White House;

(2) in any event, they'll outlast whatever period of Democratic control ensues (i.e., the mirror of the Ginsburg gamble);

(3) they've all but publicly committed themselves to staying on for now (Justice Alito says he will stay on through this term and Justice Thomas may want to pass Justice Douglas' record tenure, which would happen in May 2028); and/or

(4) a lame-duck retirement immediately after an electoral defeat would be seen as an unseemly concession to the sort of overtly political behavior by judges they've long publicly decried.

Progressives may dismiss this last consideration. Many critics see Thomas and Alito as essentially unscrupulous political actors who wouldn't hesitate to time their retirements in order to preserve another generation of conservative control. But that assumes they understand their own judicial behavior the way their harshest critics understand it. I doubt they do.

They may regard voting in accordance with their understanding of the Constitution—even when the results consistently advance conservative policy objectives—as fundamentally different from announcing their retirements right after voters have elected a Democratic Senate. On this view, they might think the former is acceptable judicial behavior while the latter is not.

On the other hand, they could see strategic retirements, which are hardly unprecedented among justices, as distinguishable from the politicized judging they've denounced. Choosing the circumstances and timing of retirement is compatible with their judicial philosophies. And many conservatives might well applaud their retirement decisions as responsible constitutional stewardship.

But a retirement announced immediately after the election to permit the outgoing Republican majority to confirm a successor, would be unusually conspicuous. Whatever their views about strategic retirement as a general matter, I'm guessing Thomas and Alito would regard the reputation cost to the Court—and to themselves—under these circumstances as too high.

The irony is that Ginsburg's cautionary example supplies the strongest argument for Thomas and Alito to retire, but also a good reason to doubt they actually will. Justices may be political actors in some respects, but they are not necessarily the political instruments their allies wish them to be.

#7747. How to Test Your Home’s Water Quality

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:05 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

We use water every day for drinking, cooking, cleaning, and bathing, but how often do we stop to think about what’s actually in it? Water that looks clean can contain potentially harmful contaminants, including lead, bacteria, and chemicals. The good news is, learning how to test water quality at home is pretty straightforward, whether you’re using an inexpensive DIY test kit, or you mail a sample to a certified laboratory. We’ll walk you through the testing process, explain what your results mean, and help you figure out what to do if you find a problem.

Even if your water looks clean doesn’t always mean it’s safe to drink. Contaminants and certain bacteria can be in there without changing the water’s appearance, taste, or smell. Testing your water helps identify potential health risks and gives you a clearer picture of what’s coming out of your faucets.

“A common misconception is that water is safe if it looks, smells and tastes fine,” says Dr. Eric Roy, Chief of Science at Culligan International. “But the reality is that contaminants such as lead, arsenic, and ‘forever chemicals’ (PFAS) cannot be detected by our senses.”

Water testing can also reveal less serious issues, such as high mineral content. Hard water, which contains elevated levels of calcium and magnesium, can cause scale buildup in pipes and appliances, leave spots on dishes, and make soap less effective. Testing can also help you get to the bottom of unpleasant tastes, unusual odors, or discoloration.

Knowing what’s in your water helps you decide whether you need a filtration system, a water softener, or another treatment method. And even if your water is perfectly safe to drink, you might still want to improve its taste or overall quality.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Testing your water quality is a simple process that takes just a few minutes of hands-on work, depending on the type of test you choose. At-home water test kits give you quick results for common water-quality indicators, while mail-in laboratory tests offer more detailed information about potentially harmful contaminants.

Before getting started, read the instructions included with your test kit carefully. Different tests have different sampling requirements, and even small mistakes, such as touching the inside of a collection bottle or flushing the faucet when you shouldn’t, can affect the accuracy of your results.

The best testing method depends on what you’re looking for. Inexpensive, at-home test kits typically use strips or color-changing solutions to check for pH, chlorine, and hardness. They’re useful for identifying common water-quality issues, but generally lack the precision to detect harmful contaminants at very low concentrations.

For health-related concerns, such as lead, arsenic, bacteria, or PFAS, choose a mail-in kit analyzed by a certified laboratory. As Dr. Jess Goddard, chief science officer at SimpleLab Inc. explains, “If you’re making a health decision or about to spend money on treatment, you definitely want lab results behind it.”

Safe Home’s mail-in water test kit checks 200 qparameters, including 7 inorganics, 31 metals, and 20 pesticides and herbicides. Read the review.

Before collecting your water sample, wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water and clear the area around the faucet. Wipe away any visible dirt or debris, and remove the faucet aerator if your testing instructions require it. Some tests, particularly those for bacteria, may also require disinfecting the faucet opening before sampling.

Be careful not to introduce contaminants during preparation. Avoid touching the inside of collection bottles or their caps, and wear disposable gloves if recommended by your test kit. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as preparation requirements can vary depending on the contaminants being tested.

For many water tests, you’ll need to run cold water through the faucet for a couple of minutes before collecting your sample. This flushes out stagnant water that’s been sitting in your plumbing, helping you collect a sample representative of your incoming water supply. However, always check your kit’s instructions first, as some tests require a different approach.

“For example, some lead-testing protocols require collecting the first water from a cold tap after several hours without use,” explains Rich Razgaitis, co-founder and CEO of FloWater. “If you flush the pipes beforehand, you may wash away the very evidence you’re looking for.”

Once the faucet is prepared, collect your sample according to your test kit’s instructions. The process differs slightly depending on your testing method:

Keep your fingers away from bottle openings and inside surfaces to prevent contamination. Seal samples immediately and follow any storage or shipping instructions.

Now it’s time to test your sample. The process will depend on whether you’re using an at-home kit or sending your water to a laboratory.

Note: At-home kits aren’t always dip strips. Some use reagents, test vials, or incubation procedures for bacteria. Always follow the instructions for the specific kit you have.

Once you’ve tested your water, the next step is figuring out what the results mean. Most at-home testing kits use color-coded charts to indicate the concentration of different substances in your water, while laboratory reports provide more precise measurements, often in parts per million (ppm), parts per billion (ppb), or milligrams per liter (mg/L).

Compare your results with the reference ranges provided by the kit or laboratory, paying particular attention to any contaminants that exceed health-based guidelines. Keep in mind that detecting a substance doesn’t automatically mean your water is unsafe.

“When interpreting results, a common mistake is assuming that a detection automatically means you have a health risk,” explains Goddard. “You need to put the result in context, first, and compare the detected concentration to a health guideline to determine if there’s a problem.”

Here’s what some common water-quality findings mean and how to address them.

Water hardness measures the concentration of dissolved minerals, primarily calcium and magnesium. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, water containing 121 to 180 ppm of hardness (measured as calcium carbonate) is considered hard, while anything above 180 ppm is very hard.

Hard water is generally safe to drink, but it can cause mineral buildup in pipes, faucets, and appliances. If your results indicate hard or very hard water and you’re experiencing these problems, consider installing a water softener. These systems reduce calcium and magnesium levels to help prevent scale buildup.

iSpring’s water softener is an electronic magnetic softener that treats mineral buildup but doesn’t remove heavy metals from water. Read the review.

Lead can enter drinking water through old pipes, solder, and plumbing fixtures, particularly in older homes. There is no known safe level of lead exposure, so any detected lead deserves attention, especially in households with children.

If a lab test detects lead, use a verified safe drinking-water source while investigating the problem. Contact your water utility or local health department for guidance, and consider having your plumbing inspected. A water filter independently certified for lead reduction can help reduce exposure, but replacing lead-containing plumbing may be necessary to address the source.

Finding E. coli in drinking water is a serious concern because it indicates fecal contamination. If your test detects E. coli, stop drinking the untreated water and contact your local health department or water utility.

For private wells, a professional may recommend inspecting and disinfecting the well, followed by additional testing to confirm the water is safe. UV treatment or other disinfection systems may also be appropriate for certain ongoing bacterial problems.

Boiling water can kill many disease-causing microorganisms, but it won’t remove chemical contaminants such as lead or nitrates. Follow the specific guidance provided by your health department rather than assuming boiling will solve every water-quality problem.

Nitrates can enter groundwater through fertilizers, septic systems, and agricultural runoff. Elevated levels are particularly dangerous for infants because they can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen.

The EPA’s drinking-water limit for nitrate is 10 mg/L measured as nitrogen (NO3-N). If your results exceed this level, switch to a verified safe water source for drinking, cooking, and preparing baby formula, and consult your local health department.

A reverse osmosis system certified for nitrate reduction may be an appropriate long-term solution. Do not boil nitrate-contaminated water, as evaporation can increase the nitrate concentration.

Arsenic and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) can be present in drinking water without any noticeable change in taste, smell, or appearance. Both can pose health risks, depending on the substance and concentration.

If lab testing identifies levels above applicable health-based guidelines, use a verified safe drinking-water source while seeking advice from your health department or a qualified water-treatment professional.

Depending on the contaminant, an appropriately certified reverse osmosis or activated carbon filtration system may help. Check that the specific system has been tested and certified to reduce the substance identified in your results.

The Waterdrop G3P600 installs under the sink and has a digital display that monitors the presence of TDS in the water. Read the review.

Not every unusual result indicates a health risk. Elevated iron can cause reddish-brown staining, while chlorine may give treated municipal water an unpleasant taste or odor. High mineral concentrations can also affect how water tastes.

If testing confirms that the issue is aesthetic rather than a health concern, you may be able to address it with a relatively simple treatment system. Activated carbon filters can improve chlorine taste and odor, while specialized iron filters can help reduce staining caused by elevated iron levels.

“A filter that improves taste isn’t necessarily removing lead,” says Razgaitis. “A water softener addresses hardness, not every health concern. UV treatment targets microorganisms but doesn’t remove dissolved chemicals.”

Whatever your results show, choose a treatment system that is independently certified to address the specific contaminants in your water, rather than assuming any filter will do the job.

Testing your home’s water quality is a simple but important step toward making sure the water you use every day is safe. Whether you use an at-home testing kit or send a sample to a certified laboratory, following the proper collection instructions will help you get reliable results.

Remember: Not every unusual reading indicates a health risk, but potentially harmful contaminants should always be taken seriously. Once you understand what’s in your water, you can make informed decisions about whether filtration, water softening, or other treatment is necessary.

Yes, you can test your home’s water quality using an at-home testing kit. Most kits use test strips or chemical reagents to check for common water-quality indicators such as pH, chlorine, and hardness. However, DIY kits have limitations, particularly when detecting potentially harmful contaminants at very low concentrations. For more comprehensive testing, the EPA recommends using a state-certified drinking water laboratory.

Common signs of poor water quality include unusual tastes or odors, cloudy or discolored water, and staining around sinks and faucets. White, chalky residue on fixtures can also indicate hard water. However, these symptoms don’t necessarily mean your water is unsafe. According to the CDC, harmful germs and chemicals may be present without affecting how water looks, tastes, or smells.

At-home water tests are a convenient, inexpensive way to screen for basic water-quality issues, such as hardness, pH, and chlorine levels. However, laboratory testing is generally the better option if you’re concerned about contaminants such as lead, arsenic, PFAS, or bacteria. These tests require greater accuracy and sensitivity than most DIY kits can provide. For example, the CDC recommends using a state-certified laboratory to test private well water.

There’s no single list of five indicators that covers every drinking-water concern, but homeowners should pay particular attention to total coliform bacteria, nitrates, pH, total dissolved solids (TDS), and lead.

#7746. How To Spot a Flood-Damaged Car Before You Buy It

Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.

With the average cost of a new car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used. But, while the lower price point is appealing, mechanic David Martin says to shop carefully and to check any used car for signs of flooding. “Engine computers, sensors, electrical connectors and wiring are vulnerable to corrosion, expensive to fix and could endanger lives,” he says. Not all cars that have been in a flood will be given a flood title, and unscrupulous sellers will mask this fact from would-be buyers. Ahead, learn how to tell if you’re buying a flood-damaged car, with expert-backed advice from Martin.

Use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle. “If the car smells musty or moldy, watch out,” Martin says. “Also, pay attention to cars that have strong air freshener or detergent scents. They could be used to mask flood-related mildew.” Additionally, look for silt or mud in glove compartments or under seats where it may have been overlooked during cleaning. Finding it is a tell-tale sign the car has been flooded. Also look carefully for condensation behind instrument panels and interior and exterior lights.

Check for any rust or flaking metal on the car’s underside, especially on brake lines and around the fuel tank, Martin says. Lift the hood and look for corrosion on the battery terminals and engine components, then open the car doors and inspect the door hinges for signs of rust.

Vehicle upholstery and carpeting can reveal signs of flooding. Feel for dampness and look for stains, as well as loose, wrinkled or buckled carpeting. Additionally, pull seat belts all the way out to check for stains, mildew or mud and look for mismatched or recently replaced carpeting and upholstery.

Turn on the car and do a thorough test of the car’s electrical components. Check the power windows, door locks, seat controls, and backup camera. “Make sure all lights, the air conditioner, heater, wipers, turn signals, stereo and navigation systems work,” Martin says. “And test them more than once.” Even if an electrical component is working, check to make sure it’s working properly. Flickering lights and intermittent functioning can also be signs of water damage.

Flood-damaged cars may be moved across state lines and retitled, so always get a Carfax report, which tracks a vehicle’s complete history regardless of location. Additionally, run the vehicle’s VIN number through the National Insurance Crime Bureau. “The service can identify whether a car has been reported stolen or labeled as salvage by insurance companies due to flooding,” Martin says. “But, while these reports can be helpful, they don’t cover everything.That’s why having a certified mechanic inspect a used car before you buy is a smart investment.”

Even if you don’t suspect a car has been flooded after looking it over yourself, a professional mechanic could catch subtle signs you missed, as well as any other mechanical issues with the vehicle. Ask them to specifically check for signs of flooding.

Yes, a flood-damaged car can still have a clean title and show no record of flooding in its history.

No, not if you intend to drive it. Issues can continue to arise years after a flooding event that can impact the vehicle’s functioning. However, you could buy a flooded car with the intention of using it for parts.

#7744. If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

Cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

Colored lights play an important part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

But what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

Cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

On Oct. 23, NHTSA announced a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to update safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”

“As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”

Cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

Mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The company has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

“Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the company said in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

Those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the new federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

Designed to keep drinks piping hot for up to 90 minutes in the mug or all day on the charging coaster, the Ember Mug 2 is the perfect way to elevate your loved one’s sipping experience. It can keep drinks pleasantly warm as well, since users can set the temperature between 120 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit.

What our tester says: “The Ember Mug 2 excels at its central job: keeping liquid hot. As long as I maintained a connection between the mug and my iPhone via Bluetooth while the mug was full, my coffee’s temperature never fluctuated from the exact temperature I selected.”—Lizzy Briskin, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Ember mug (various colors) at Amazon, Walmart, or Target.

A must-have for drinks on the deck or by the backyard fire pit, the Yeti Rambler Cocktail Shaker brings heavy-duty insulation to outdoor mixology. The leak-resistant lid and twist-cap prevent mess-making while shaking, and the main tumbler doubles as a durable hot- or cold-beverage vessel when you’re not whipping up highballs and martinis.

Recognized as one of the BobVila.com team’s 2026 Home Hero Award winners, the Cosori Iconic air fryer was built to enhance everyday cooking. Homebodies can stay warm all winter with our pick for the best electric heater. Few things say “cozy night in” like a pot of soup or stew simmering on the stove. Dimmable and color-changing, these Philips Hue Smart Bulbs are a simple solution to all your lighting needs. Most homebodies have some type of cozy home routine, and these affordable but endlessly useful TP-Link Tapo P125M Mini Smart Wi-Fi Plugs can help automate it. Homebodies can skip the late-night run to the store with the KitchenAid Ice Cream Maker Attachment. It’s a fun gift for anyone who already owns the mixer and would rather experiment with flavors from their own kitchen than wait in line at the ice cream shop.

What our tester says: “We love ice cream in our house, and this attachment exceeded all of my expectations. It’s simple to use, and within 20 minutes you have delicious, homemade ice cream. You can customize any recipe, and one batch makes enough for four people. Once you’re finished, cleaning takes 30 seconds, and you pop it back in the freezer for your next batch.”—Stephanie Cronk, Executive Editor of Product Reviews

Reading, crafting, and lounging can all be more comfortable with this supportive Nestl Reading Pillow. Stuffed with high-density shredded memory foam, it contours to your back and arms to prevent slouching whether you’re sitting up in bed or relaxing on the floor. The soothing heat function gently eases tight joints and improves circulation, and the adjustable straps secure it to your chair for hands-free use.

Convincing homebodies to come outside (at least to the backyard) is easier with the Solo Stove Bonfire 2.0, which features a smokeless flame that makes any cleared yard area or patio extra cozy. As the top pick in our best outdoor doormats guide, this heavy-duty doormat from L.L.Bean is designed to handle even the busiest and messiest of entryways. Constructed from durable recycled polyester with a sturdy rubber backing, it features a water-dam border that helps it hold up to 1.5 gallons of water per square yard without leaking. During our hands-on tests, it did an excellent job trapping dirt and moisture from passing pets and pedestrians before they could track inside.

What our tester says: “I liked how easy this doormat was to clean. I shook off dry debris, rinsed the mat with a hose, and it looked like new.”—Stacey L. Nash, Product Reviews tester and writer

A garden of twittering birds can make a home feel all the more quaint, and your giftee can attract feathered friends with the Brome Squirrel Solution200 Squirrel-proof Bird Feeder. As the best bird feeder in our testing, it lived up to its squirrel-proof claims, thwarting squirrels while providing an attractive space for small birds to perch.

What our tester says: “This feeder performed well in testing. It successfully foiled squirrels over and over again. The size and design are perfect for small bird species such as house finches and chickadees.”—Debbie Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Hugging laundry fresh from the dryer is always a cozy experience, so why not step out of your bath or shower into a warm towel every time? With Zadro’s bucket towel warmer, you can. As one of the best towel warmers from our tests, this spacious model heats up to two extra-large bath towels, throw blankets, or sweaters to toasty in minutes. Plus, there’s a built-in timer so you can set customizable heating intervals as well as an automatic shut-off for safety and peace of mind.

Get the Zadro towel warmer at Amazon, Target, or Crate & Barrel.

If your homebody giftee is an avid home cook, the Vego Kitchen Composter is a fabulous choice—especially if they’re also tight on space. As a compact countertop composter, it turns kitchen scraps into usable compost, and since it has smart features alongside its manual controls, it was an easy pick as this year’s best electric composter.

What our tester says: “The composter’s efficiency is remarkable, offering four modes so you can choose the ideal setting for your needs. I primarily use the eco mode, which breaks down food in just a few hours, then add the byproduct to my outdoor composting bin to complete the composting process.”—Debbie Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Read our full review: Vego Kitchen Composter

Get the Vego composter at Amazon, Wayfair, or Vego.

#7742. Full Court Denies DOJ Petition In California Election Case In About 7 Hours, No Reply Needed

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Justice Kagan likely orchestrated the shadow execution before the petition was even filed.

I think we have seen a new record for speed on the emergency docket. Today, shortly before noon, the Solicitor General filed an emergency application in the California election law case. The brief was about 20 pages long. Circuit Justice never even bothered calling for a response. Shortly before 7:00, the petition was referred to the full Court, and was denied.

Rick Hasen calls it a mercy killing. I think shadow execution is more appropriate.

Indeed, this ruling was likely orchestrated by Circuit Justice Kagan before the petition was even filed. The government's case was dead on arrival. And Kagan spared California the fate that befell Missouri, which had to file a pointless brief that no one would read.

NEXT: Will Alito or Thomas Retire if Democrats Win the Senate?

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7740. The Best Holiday Decorations Across the U.S., and How to Steal the Look

These homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

Outdoor holiday decorating is an art. And while we love a tasteful string of white Christmas lights or a few pumpkins placed by the front door, why not really go for it when the holiday season rolls around? Over-the-top outdoor holiday decorations make the whole neighborhood get in the festive spirit! To help inspire you, we found some of the best maximalist holiday homes from coast to coast.

From extra spooky Halloween displays to dazzling Christmas spectacles, these homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

A post shared by jessica archibald (@jessicarchibald)

Halloween 2026 has come and gone, but it’s never too early to start thinking about next year! Known simply as The Pumpkin House, @jessicarchibald lines her roof, porch, and yard with hundreds of jack-o’-lanterns every Halloween season. The piles of pumpkins make a big impact both during the day and at night.

Steal This Idea: All you need is pumpkins! Attach faux pumpkins to long boards to make them easier to display on the roof.

The Kraken House (@krakenhousenola) captured here by @amournola, uses blow-up decor to explore the haunted seas. The blow-up tentacles hint at a sea monster hiding beyond the windows, but the dramatic lighting is what really makes this house shine.

Steal This Idea: Skip the kid-friendly Bluey holiday inflatable this year, and attach these terrifying tentacles instead. Then turn up the drama with solar up-lights in green and purple.

Can you believe this amazing black cat is a DIY project? To transform this front porch into a Halloween stage, @allset_bygabrielle hand-carved the cat figure out of wood and painted every detail.

Steal This Idea: In addition to the vintage-inspired cat, the spooky forest framing the door was made with a mix of dead branches and faux botanicals; providing texture and a subtle sparkle.

This front entry in New York City (photographed by @victoria.nycvisit) uses dark drapery, black roses, and a wide variety of unique pumpkins and squashes to create a gothic masterpiece. Trick-or-treaters beware!

Steal This Idea: It’s amazing what a few swathes of black and burgundy fabric can do. Drape the fabric around your front door to make an eerie entrance. Then use pumpkins and vases full of dark flowers to complete the look.

This viral townhouse @stoopandthecity, is dressed to the nines for every holiday. This autumn harvest display features patterned pumpkins and cascades of fall foliage. It’s perfect for Thanksgiving or for those that prefer to skip the ghosts and goblins.

Steal This Idea: Choose faux and glass pumpkins in a cohesive color scheme, and don’t hold back on the fall foliage. Use faux stems to make the display last all season long.

A post shared by Marissa Fiala | Houston, TX (@houstonhotspots)

When it comes to Christmas lights, you can’t find much better than the extravagant homes in the River Oaks neighborhood of Houston, Texas. Each home goes all out with sparkling lights on its exterior, wrapped around every tree.

Steal This Idea: The secret to this colorful tree, captured by @houstonhotspots, is wrapping the lights tightly around the trunk and every single branch. The technique takes time but makes a big impact. Use LED lights to cut back on electricity use.

This famous house on Castro Street in San Francisco does not hold back! (Photo by @415urbanadventures.) Every exterior surface is covered in decor. The symmetrical layout keeps it looking classy instead of gaudy. And of course, the star of the show is Santa hanging in the middle, ready to deliver gifts.

Steal This Idea: The key element of this display is the garland covered in shiny Christmas ornaments. When you think you’ve gathered enough baubles, you’ll probably need even more!

The historic mill in Clifton, Ohio, is known for its over-the-top Christmas light display, featuring over four million lights! While you might not have a historic mill to decorate, the lighting techniques can be used on your own home to dazzle the entire neighborhood.

Steal This Idea: The most memorable element of this display is the iconic red lights cascading down the hillside. Try laying strings lights in rows along your entire yard to get a similar look.

A post shared by Joe Yost | Yost Team -Compass Pittsburgh (@joeyostteam)

Make your house look like one giant Christmas present by adding a larger-than-life red bow. This Pittsburgh mansion is famous for its red Christmas bow that looks beautifully whimsical in the daytime and lights up at night.

Steal This Idea: You don’t need a mansion to recreate this look. Get your own giant red bow and hang it above your front door. Here’s one available on Etsy!

A post shared by Pink Dreams Collection (@pinkdreamscollection)

One way to set your house apart for Christmas is to use a non-traditional color scheme —like pink! This darling cottage from @pinkdreamcollection is a frosted pink confection complete with pink trees and pink nutcracker figurines.

Steal This Idea: Pink or pastel Christmas decor will make your home look playful and unique. Use different shades of pink to add dimension.

A post shared by The Hazard’s Gingerbread House (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse)

This spectacular residential light display by Walter Hazard (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse) makes his home look like a technicolor gingerbread house. The secret is the wire-fencing frames he uses to create methodical light patterns. Visitors come from all over the area to witness the gorgeous lights in action.

Steal This Idea: We might not all have the same light-manipulation talent as Walter, but you can get the same grid-like coverage with LED curtain lights like these.

#7739. Want Year-Round Curb Appeal, Even in Winter? Try These 20 Stunning Plants

By Jennifer Noonan, Updated by Teresa Odle

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Does your home’s landscape look barren and brown after autumn leaves fall, and doesn’t perk back up again until spring? Most homeowners think about how their beds will look when they’re in full bloom, but few imagine how that same bed will look in the dead of winter. Outdoor winter plants that add beautiful contrast to a snowy landscape aren’t just good for your curb appeal—they can also provide critical food sources and nesting sites for wildlife. As you consider updates to the plants and shrubs that surround your home, look to these appealing, year-round options.

Blue Ice bog rosemary’s unique silvery-blue foliage looks good in every season, plus this evergreen ground cover delights with a shock of pink bell-shaped blooms in early spring. Perfect for rock gardens and moist soils, it will attract birds and bring visual interest to the yard all year.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 6Size: 1 to 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Blue Ice Bog Rosemary at The Tree Center for $39.50

This dwarf pine variety turns from green to gold when cold weather arrives. In fact, the colder the climate, the more intense its color becomes. This rabbit- and deer-resistant plant is easy to care for, and an evergreen shrub that will look beautiful all year long. It grows slowly, but immediately adds low-growing color and texture to a winter bed.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 7Size: nearly 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted Carstens Wintergold Mugo Pine at Mike’s Plants on Etsy for $75

Many weeping ornamentals lose their leaves in cold weather, but not the weeping Norway spruce. With its unusual shape and showy cones, this evergreen makes a great accent in the garden and provides rich green in all four seasons. It can thrive in many soil types, including rich sandy soils, and has low water needs once established.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: 4 feet high and 15 feet aroundWhere to buy: Get a 3- to 4-foot high Weeping Norway Spruce at Spring Hill Nurseries for $299

This evergreen succulent creates a lush and attractive carpet that thrives year-round in cool to warm climates. Most boast tiny flowers that attract butterflies in summer, and the foliage of Pink Form and Purple Form can take on reddish to purple hues in colder months. Easy to care for in full sun, this little wonder packs a lot of life in its compact height but excellent spread. After a season or two, it is xeric.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 9Size: 1 feet high and 1 to 1.5 feet aroundWhere to buy: Get a 4-inch pot of Sedum Hispanicum at Cristina’s Garden on Etsy for $10.99

For evergreen ground cover in warmer climates, try Pot Belly Pittosporum. The tough little shrub flowers in spring and summer, leaving its silvery green foliage with a white underside on the plant through winter.  Best of all, it keeps its rounded shape with little maintenance required. Pot Belly Pittosporum is drought tolerant once established and can grow in partial to full sun.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 8 to 11Size: 4 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Pot Belly Pittosporum at Cornell Farm for $28.99

This ground-hugging variety of dianthus is evergreen and cold hardy. Its gray-green foliage erupts in summer with flowers, making it a wonderful filler both in the garden and in pots, so feel free to grow it in a container and overwinter it indoors in colder zones. The flowers are also fragrant, adding a clove-like scent to the garden.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: about 1 foot high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Frosty Fire Dianthus at Holly Days for $11.99

If you’re looking for a distinctive shade of evergreen color, dwarf globe blue spruce delivers. This slow-growing, densely branched conifer has blue needles that become more brilliant in summer. It makes a wonderful low hedge, or stands out as a small rabbit-resistant shrub.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 4 to 8Size: 2 to 3 feet high and 3 to 4 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Dwarf Globe Blue Spruce tree at Trees.com for $54.95

Pink pussytoe plants provide an evergreen mat of tiny silver-gray leaves. In late spring, the plant spikes deep pink, fuzzy flowers. It’s a slow grower and requires little water once established, so this cold-hardy beauty is a breeze to care for in any season. The native cultivar grows best in full sun.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: 0.5 feet high and 1 foot wideWhere to buy: Get a bag of 20 Pussytoes seeds at SeedCult on Etsy for $2.99

Snowdrop bulbs are happiest with cold or moderate winters, and are among favorite winter-flowering plants. Place them in full or partial where you can enjoy their delicate white flowers in the fall and throughout the cold months, even during snow. Come spring, they’ll go dormant.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 9Size: 0.5 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a bag of 25 Galanthus Nivalis bulbs at White Flower Farm for $20

Christmas rose, a variety of hellebore, is a pest-resistant evergreen perennial. It also provides valuable nectar for early pollinators, like the rusty patched bumblebee, who are seeking blooms in late winter or early spring. Find it a shady location with space to grow, and soon you’ll enjoy its white winter blooms in the warmer end of their growing range or early spring where colder.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: 1 foot tall and up to 1.5 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted Ivory Prince Christmas Rose at Plant Addicts for $49.99

Winter jasmine is a vining shrub that will treat you with bursts of fragrant yellow flowers between late winter and early spring; the plant’s flowers often are the first to appear as winter wraps up. But even when not in bloom, this plant’s large arching stems will provide plenty of visual interest to the garden. Hardy and easy to grow, winter jasmine is just at home in coastal areas as it is along rock walls.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 10Size: up to 10 feet tall and 6 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon pot of Winter Jasmine at The Home Depot for $25.58

Known for its medicinal properties, witch hazel is often used in cosmetics and lotions, since it is reported to reduce inflammation and soothe certain skin irritations. It’s also a great choice for a winter garden, thanks to its fragrant yellow-to-red flowers that can bloom even in snowy weather. This adaptable shrub or small tree thrives in full sun to partial shade.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: 3 to 6 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1- to 2-foot high Witch Hazel at TN Nursery for $26.99

Named for its small clusters of white berries that put on a show throughout the winter and give way to little white flowers in the spring, the snowberry plant provides a valuable food source for birds during the cold winter months. This easy-care plant will spread as a dense thicket, so it’s a great choice for borders and living fences.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 9Size: more than 15 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted White Snowberry at The Home Depot for $38.04

Featuring dark green glossy leaves, sweet box plants are shade-loving evergreen shrubs that boast small fragrant flowers that bloom in late winter and early spring. Once the fragrant flowers fade, little black fruits will appear in their wake. Preferring partial to full shade, sweet box plants are tough and excellent year-round plants to add interest to the garden.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 8Size: up to 2 feet high and 4 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Fragrant Dwarf Sweet Box at Planting Partners on Etsy for $28.99

For a vibrant splash of color in warmer zones, plant winter heath in your yard, which will repay you with abundant tiny pink winter flowers that bloom in late winter through early spring. The colorful winter shrub is an even hardier version of E. carnea, and both are commonly used as a ground cover, forming a dense mat. Prune it right after it finishes flowering in the spring to prevent leafless stems and keep it looking great all year.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 8Size: up to 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a quart-size potted Erica Kramer’s Red Winter Heath at The Home Depot for $18.53

This deciduous shrub’s large size creates a show-stopping garden accent. In mid- to late fall, the American cranberry bush will burst with vibrant red berries that last into winter. The berries  are edible but aren’t very tasty when eaten raw. However, they provide important winter food for wildlife. Fragrant while flowers appear in spring and persist through mid summer. The shrub thrives in full or partial sun and prefers alkaline soil.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 7Size: 8 to 12 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 3-gallon Bailey Compact American Cranberry Bush at Plant Addicts for $73.99

Also known as Perovskia, Russian sage is popular for its tall blue-violet flowers that bloom in the summer through the fall, attracting all sorts of pollinators to the garden. However, this shrub looks great in the winter, too, thanks to long silvery stems that offer structure and intrigue to a winter landscape. Leave the faded flower stems on until new growth appears in spring and plant Russian sage along walkways to maximize enjoyment of its fragrant flowers in summer. Once established, it is a drought-tolerant shrub.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 9Size: up to 4 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 3-inch potted Lacey Blue Russian Sage at American Meadows for $7.99

Also known as Eastern teaberry, American wintergreen features glossy evergreen leaves and bright red berries that will offer a beautiful contrast to a wintery white landscape. Like many winter outdoor plants, this shrub helps small mammals and birds who love the berries. It is disease-resistant, and crushing its leaves will release a refreshing wintergreen scent. Plant the showy low grower in dappled sunlight to deep shade to keep it happy.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: less than 1 foot high and up to 1 foot wideWhere to buy: Get 6 bare root Teaberry Wintergreen plants at New Hampshire Plants on Etsy for $9.99

Yucca glauca is among the most winter-hardy yucca varieties. Its attractive evergreen foliage features long narrow stems in a rosette shape that look great all year long. In the spring, a stem rises from the rosette that features white bell-shaped flowers. These flowers attract butterflies, and the entire easy-care yucca plant provides food and nesting opportunities for small mammals, birds, and reptiles.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 4 to 8Size: 3 to 4 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 5-inch pot of Soapweed Yucca at Etsy for $24.75

This low-growing shrub features glossy dark green leaves that turn bronze in the fall, persisting through the winter. During the winter you’ll also be treated to the shrub’s remaining vivid red berries, which provide a valuable food source for birds. #7738. That Hole in Your Ruler Isn’t Random – Here’s What It’s Actually For

That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history. Here's why it exists and how people use it.

Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line. But even after years of using one, there’s a small detail that’s easy to miss: the hole near the end.

Those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design. They actually serve a purpose, and the reason they’re there goes back further than most people might expect. Here’s what they’re for, how they were used in the past, and a few other ways they come in handy.

The hole at the end of a ruler is mainly there for storage. It lets people hang the ruler on a hook, nail, or pegboard instead of leaving it in a drawer or on a workbench. This is particularly helpful with longer metal rulers that might not fit in a toolbox.

But the hole has been around for much longer than modern workshops. Years ago, before paper notebooks became common in schools, students practiced writing on small slate boards. They could wipe away their writing with a damp cloth and use the board again.

Some students tied that cloth to their rulers with a piece of string through the hole. That way, they always had something nearby to clean their slates. Schools eventually moved away from slate boards, but the holes remained. Today, they’re mostly there to make rulers easier to hang and store.

Hanging a ruler isn’t the only reason manufacturers add holes. Some rulers have several, and they can serve different purposes depending on where they’re placed. For example, certain school rulers have three holes spaced along one side. These line up with the rings in a standard three-ring binder, so students can keep their rulers with their other school supplies.

Some rulers also have holes that help with drawing circles. A pin through one hole can hold the ruler in place while a pencil in another hole traces a circle as the ruler turns. Not every ruler has holes designed for this, but specialty models like the Creative Grids Quick Trim Ruler do. A compass is still a better choice when exact measurements matter.

Some crafting rulers have holes for more specific jobs. Quilting rulers and templates may have openings that help mark circles or line up fabric before cutting. Others have slots or shaped edges that guide a rotary cutter, making it easier to cut certain shapes.

There are also special rulers for paper crafts and stitching. Some have rows of tiny, evenly spaced holes that help people mark where to make stitches or decorative patterns.

Of course, not every ruler has holes. Smaller plastic rulers often don’t need them, while longer metal versions may have one at each end. It mostly comes down to how the manufacturer expects people to use the ruler. And for everyday measuring, the holes don’t make much difference. A ruler without them can measure just as accurately as one with them.

Furnace and air conditioner filters are integral to the ongoing operation of the HVAC system, so it’s important to find out what you might not know about HVAC air filters. Learning more about air filters for furnace filtration can help you determine what to look for when choosing a furnace filter’s replacement, including the type of air filter and MERV rating, as well as furnace and air conditioner filter sizes.
